extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scholarly-communication practitioners, platform designers, journal editors and policy makers interested in alternatives and innovations in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and design criteria for next-generation peer review and scholarly-evaluation platforms, comparing features of social/web systems (Reddit, Amazon, Stack Exchange, GitHub, Wikipedia) and their pros/cons for scholarly use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality control and moderation, possibly through openness and transparency
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed as a key feature for any future peer review platform; can be implemented via community moderators (e.g., subreddit mods), editorial roles, or automated filters. Benefits include responsibility, accountability and improved quality; risks include censorship, peer pressure, and lowering of quality if misapplied. Moderation must balance openness with filtering of inappropriate behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification via personalized reputation or performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Certification via personalized reputation or performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reputation/karma/badges to certify reviewer contributions and provide prestige. Can be personalized and visible on profiles. Must be carefully designed so reputation reflects behavior not just popularity; tying to durable identity infrastructures (e.g., ORCID) improves robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive structures to motivate and encourage engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Incentive structures to motivate and encourage engagement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incentives can be badges, monetary reward, recognition, or credit that is citable/re-usable. Examples include Center for Open Science badges and paid or token-based systems (Blockchain). Risks: monetization/perverted incentives, expense, and gaming. Incentives should align with scholarly values and be balanced against gaming risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting or rating (quantified review evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voting or rating: Quantified review evaluation (5 stars, points), including up- and down-votes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a community-driven, simple quality filter and efficient sorting. Implementations include up/down votes (Reddit) and 5-star scales (Amazon/ScienceOpen). Risks: randomized auto-promotion/down-promotion, gaming, popularity bias, non-static assessments, and lack of contextual justification for ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness (public visibility of review content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness: Public visibility of review content
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reviews increase responsibility, accountability, and provide context; can raise quality and transparency. Downsides include peer pressure, retaliation, potential reduction in candid critiques, and possible lower-quality contributions if reviewers self-censor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation (reviewer evaluation and ranking: points, review statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation: Reviewer evaluation and ranking (points, review statistics)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation systems act as a quality filter and provide rewards/motivation. They can upgrade privileges (as on Stack Exchange) and be used to weight influence. Beware imbalance based on user status, platform-specific artifacts, and gaming; single-formula reputations are vulnerable to manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public commenting (visible comments on paper/review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public commenting: Visible comments on paper/review
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables living/organic papers, community involvement, progressive development, and inclusivity. Drawbacks include potential for harassment, being time-consuming, low interoperability with other systems, and limited re-use of comments unless archived and structured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Version control (managed releases and configurations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Version control: Managed releases and configurations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports living/iterative documents that are verifiable and progressive; aids organization and traceability of changes. Issues include citation tracking complexities, increased time overhead, and potential low trust of constantly changing content unless clearly versioned and archived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication and certification (filtering contributors via verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentication and certification: Filtering of contributors via verification process
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification (e.g., ORCID-backed checks) can provide fraud control, protect authors, and stabilize the system. Risks include hacking, management difficulty, and potential exclusion of legitimate contributors if verification is onerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation (filtering inappropriate behaviour in comments/rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation: Filtering of inappropriate behaviour in comments and ratings
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community-driven moderation can maintain quality and civility (Reddit/Stack Exchange models). However, moderation risks being viewed as censorship and can suppress marginalized voices; governance of moderation must be transparent and accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating engagement into prestige (karma, graded ratings, ranking algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translating engagement into prestige: Use of karma points, graded ratings, and ranking algorithms to confer prestige
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems can aggregate upvotes/downvotes or star ratings into profiles and metrics, and rank content via algorithms combining quality, relevance, and recency. Considerations include making metrics commensurate with effort, ensuring community/assessment bodies value them, and designing algorithms to mitigate popularity bias (e.g., combining quality, relevance, recency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom-of-crowds limits and the Principle of Multiple Magnifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom-of-crowds concerns: quantity versus quality and the Principle of Multiple Magnifications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd-sourced review assumes many participants will yield optimal assessment, but expertise varies and self-selection can bias outcomes. The Principle of Multiple Magnifications suggests more reviewers and more metadata about them improves results, but platforms must capture and archive consensus points for external reuse and consider when to constrain review to reach consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of 'the rich get richer' and editorial balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk that prominent researchers dominate attention ('the rich get richer')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-profile authors may receive disproportionate engagement and hype. Mitigations include empowered core editors/moderators who can invite peers, curate, and promote under-noticed but worthy contributions; intelligent crowd reviewing (editorial seeding) can improve fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star-rating system pitfalls (positivity bias, skew, popularity over quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Star-rating pitfalls: positivity skew, selection for popularity rather than quality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five-star scales are widespread but often skew positive (average ~4.3), and can favor popularity. Star ratings alone lack contextual justification; they should be paired with textual reviews, provenance, and weighting to be useful in scholarly evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing the reviewers / meta-evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing the reviewers: voting on review helpfulness and weighting reviewers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems can allow community 'helpful' votes on reviews, elevate spotlight reviewers, and weight ratings by rater reputation to foster good behavior and penalize bad. Alternatives include decentralized digital signatures linking reviewers to papers to build a web-of-trust resistant to gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stack Exchange-style QA mechanics (voting, accepted answers, thread closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stack Exchange mechanics: questions, focused answers, voting, accepted answers, and thread closure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages concise problem-focused exchanges, community curation of top answers, and closure once resolved, reducing evaluation load. Reputation and privileges incentivize participation. Adaptation to peer review must handle that new research materials (novel contributions) are not typically the focus on QA sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Badge acquisition and tag badges as expertise indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Badge acquisition: merit badges and tag badges as public stamps of affiliation, experience and expertise
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Badges function as motivational targets and local qualitative signals of expertise (including subject-level tag badges). They can broaden recognition beyond publications but may be platform-specific and gamable.

rubrics_metrics.name: GitHub-style social code-review features (issues, notifications, labels, checklists)
rubrics_metrics.description: GitHub features: issue-based discussions, notifications, tagging/labels, checklists, assignments and organizations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features support fine-grained, traceable review tasks, allow contributors to watch updates, assign responsibility, and manage review checklists. They support collaborative iteration and make review activities discoverable and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: GitHub-enabled attribution and metrics (stars, forks, tracked contributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: GitHub attribution: public contributions, stars/forks/watchers as prestige metrics and tracked contribution histories
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public commits and forks enable measurable prestige and reuse signals; tracked contributions let reviewers claim credit and measure impact. This can shift prestige toward engagement and reuse rather than journal branding, but can privilege types of work that suit Git workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive iterative peer review using version control
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive iterative peer review: version control facilitates repeated review iterations, transparency and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Version control allows reviewers to assess methods/data/code comprehensively, encourages small focused tasks for reviewers, and keeps a history of changes. It supports post-publication review and reduces rejection bias by aiming to work with authors until items are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete Git-based review workflow (JOSS example: issue-as-review, checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete GitHub workflow (example from JOSS): submission → pre-review issue → topic editor → review issue with checklist → reviewers check off elements → iterative fixes until checklist resolved
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a lightweight, transparent, iterative review mechanism where checklists define required elements, editor manages assignment and disputes, and the review issue remains linked to the published submission for provenance and reuse. This model emphasizes acceptance-through-fix rather than rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host-neutral standards for Git-based peer review (prescribed directory structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Host-neutral Git standards: use of a prescribed directory structure for peer review artifacts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: standardize directory layouts (e.g., manuscript_version_1/peer_reviews) to enable interoperability and host neutrality across Git platforms. This aids automation, discoverability, and reuse of review materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public identity options for contributions (signed, pseudonymous, anonymized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public identity options: comments and reviews may be signed by default, pseudonymous, or anonymized until revealed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing multiple identity modes supports different norms and safety needs. Systems should offer filters (e.g., hide anonymized comments) and back-end verification (ORCID/email) so users can choose privacy while enabling accountability when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threaded/nested commenting and presentation of highest-ranked content
rubrics_metrics.description: Threaded/nested commenting with ranking: nested discussions with top-ranked comments shown first
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nested threads allow focused sub-discussions and tracking of conversations; sorting by score highlights high-value contributions. Consider retention/archiving of consensus branches and mechanisms to surface context-rich comments rather than only popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikipedia-style collective-authoring dynamics (iterative edits, anonymous volunteers, authorship complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wikipedia model: continuous reworking and updating by largely anonymous volunteers, leading to cumulative iterative improvements
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective intelligence can scale content creation and improvement, but complicates attribution and authorship. Platforms adopting this model must address credit, version provenance, and motivations for sustained contribution (altruism vs recognition).
